brand.title: ESourceAIG (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — AI Decisions at Work

questions.question: According to the course, what is the core gap that causes AI-assisted decisions to go wrong in organizations?
choices: Organizations choose AI tools that are not powerful enough for their needs.
The space between what an AI tool produces and the judgment required to act on it responsibly.
Employees do not have enough training time allocated to learning new software.
AI tools are intentionally designed to be difficult to use in workplace settings.
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the course frames the problem not as a tool deficiency but as a judgment gap that structured learning is designed to close.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course distinguishes between the tool itself and the human judgment required to use it responsibly. Review Slide 3 to see how the instructor frames this dynamic.

questions.question: What does the Harvard Business School case study reveal about the relationship between tool access and proficiency?
choices: Access to AI tools automatically creates proficiency among all learners.
Engagement data like login rates and tool usage tell you whether decisions actually improved.
Reported engagement (51% tutorbot use, 100% Julius.ai use) measures whether people opened the tools, not whether decisions got better.
Tool proficiency requires only a one-time orientation from faculty.
questions.feedback_correct: You have identified the critical distinction the course makes: engagement metrics show presence, not performance or decision quality.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The HBS example is central to understanding why engagement data alone is misleading. Reread Slide 4 to see what the high usage percentages actually measure.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why only 12% of learners in the HBS accounting course became frequent tutorbot users?
choices: The accounting discipline is inherently less suited to AI assistance than other fields.
Unresolved policy uncertainty, accuracy concerns, and unclear governance caused people to default to caution.
The tutorbot was designed specifically for MBA students and was too advanced for accounting learners.
Frequent tutorbot use conflicted with the course grading policies.
questions.feedback_correct: This reflects the course's finding that unclear governance directly produces avoidance—when people do not know what is permitted or who is accountable, they stop using the tool.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 5 shows that accuracy concerns and policy gaps went unresolved, leaving learners uncertain. Slide 15 makes explicit the link between unclear governance and low adoption.

questions.question: According to the course, what are the three characteristics that indicate a decision is suitable for AI assistance?
choices: The decision involves personal or interpersonal consequences, rare or unique situations, and confidential data.
Clear inputs, verifiable outputs, and some tolerance for occasional error.
High stakes, reputational risk, and accountability that cannot be transferred to a tool.
The decision requires real-time speed, involves large datasets, and affects many employees.
questions.feedback_correct: You have identified the three-part matching test correctly: work that is information-dense, repeatable, and reviewable is where AI adds reliable value.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 8 presents the matching logic: AI adds value where tasks have clear inputs and verifiable outputs. Decisions with privacy, reputational, or interpersonal stakes belong outside AI workflows.

questions.question: What does the three-part filter on Slide 9 ask you to evaluate before using AI on any decision?
choices: Whether the AI tool is the most recent version available and how many competitors use the same tool.
Verifiability of the output, accountability if the output is wrong, and whether the data is appropriate to share with the tool.
How long the AI tool has been on the market, whether employees prefer it to manual methods, and its cost relative to alternatives.
The tool's accuracy rate, the number of users in your industry, and whether it complies with ISO standards.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—these three questions form the practical decision test: Can you verify the output? Who is accountable? Is the data appropriate to share?
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 9 presents a governance-focused filter, not a technical or market-based one. The three questions center on verifiability, accountability, and data appropriateness.

questions.question: Why does the course treat accuracy as an operational problem rather than something fully solved by tool design?
choices: Because only older AI tools have accuracy problems; newer ones are perfect.
Because even well-designed institutional deployments like HBS identified accuracy as an ongoing friction point, not a one-time configuration issue.
Because accuracy can never be measured reliably in any workplace setting.
Because the course recommends avoiding AI tools entirely due to accuracy concerns.
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—even in well-resourced settings, accuracy remains a variable to manage through governance and verification, not an assumption.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 10 clarifies that accuracy is not fully solved and must be treated as a variable. The three-part filter is designed to handle this reality honestly.

questions.question: What is an example of an operational constraint that can affect AI deployment in an organization?
choices: Employees might prefer older AI tools they already know.
Harvard Business Publishing requires prior written permission and disabled data sharing before its catalog content can be used in a generative AI tool.
AI tools are generally too expensive for most organizations to afford.
The organization's internet connection might not be fast enough to run AI applications.
questions.feedback_correct: You have identified a real governance constraint: content rights and data-sharing terms are operational requirements that must be discovered and managed, not ignored.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 13 illustrates that compliance and permissions are not bureaucratic afterthoughts—they are operational constraints you discover during implementation.

questions.question: According to the escalation framework presented in the course, when should you refer an AI output upward to a superior rather than acting on it yourself?
choices: Whenever the AI output disagrees with your personal opinion.
When the decision involves accountability, privacy, or risk that exceeds your authority.
Only if the AI tool is brand new and you have not used it before.
When the output is longer than one paragraph and requires careful reading.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—the third position of the escalation framework is appropriate governance, not indecision; it protects both you and the organization.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 14 defines the three-position framework: act (low-risk, verifiable), verify (moderate stakes), and refer upward (high accountability or risk). Refer when the decision exceeds your authority.

questions.question: What is the most important evaluation question to ask before approving any AI learning program?
choices: How much will the program cost and can we get a bulk discount?
Is this program built around real decisions, or is it a technology demonstration in disguise?
How many employees are currently enrolled in competing programs?
Does the vendor offer 24/7 customer support for technical issues?
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—programs that lead with tool features rather than learner decision outcomes are product demonstrations, not learning programs.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 17 makes clear that the first priority is whether a program is actually designed to change what learners can decide, not what they can do with a tool.

questions.question: Based on the course's evaluation checklist, why is "named accountability" an essential component of any AI learning program?
choices: It ensures that someone can be blamed if the program does not work.
It provides a specific faculty member or subject-matter expert whose name is attached to the content and who is responsible for updating it.
It allows learners to file complaints directly with leadership.
It guarantees that the program will use only the most expensive AI tools available.
questions.feedback_correct: Right—named accountability ensures the program is maintained, updated, and has someone responsible for its quality and outcomes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 18 lists named accountability as a core requirement. This is about ensuring ongoing ownership and quality, not blame; it is a governance safeguard.

questions.question: What does the course recommend you require from a vendor who claims their AI learning program improves decision quality?
choices: A testimonial from one satisfied customer and their marketing brochure.
Targets set before the program launches, causal evidence beyond faculty observations, and a clear comparison to a baseline.
A promise that 100% of learners will use the AI tool after completing the program.
A guarantee that learners will never make mistakes using AI tools again.
questions.feedback_correct: You have identified the rigorous measurement standard the course insists on: pre-launch targets, causal evidence, and controlled comparison, not post-hoc claims.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Slide 20 distinguishes between observational reports (valuable but not causal evidence) and real measurement (targets set in advance, before-and-after comparison). Review that distinction.
